			18 text The Tepper School of Business, located in Pittsburgh, offers a unique MBA experience to transitioning veterans.  At Tepper, veterans are challenged, mentored, and educated to conquer the next set of challenges and prepare for a successful career outside of the military.
			19 text The Tepper MBA revolves around a vibrant and inclusive student community, which will strengthen and diversify service members' perspectives and teaming experience. This community, along with its strong alumni of network will deliver a winning network to help veterans successfully transition from the military to their next career.
		20 container

			23 text At the Tepper School of Business, veterans are quickly immersed in challenging coursework led by an energetic, engaging, and dynamic faculty. A Tepper MBA builds upon valuable military skills and experience by developing and refining business judgement throughout an extensive core curriculum. Veterans will be transformed by the exciting opportunities on campus at one of the top engineering and technology universities in the world, and the abundant energy of thriving Pittsburgh will make every day unique and exciting.

			27 text The mission of the Tepper Veterans Association is to support transitioning service members and veterans, both U.S. and international, who are interested in pursuing an MBA. 			51 text Becoming a member of the Bangladeshi Student Organization (BSO) at CMU offers students a chance to connect with a supportive and vibrant community. Members can celebrate traditional Bangladeshi festivals such as Eid, Pohela Boishakh, and International Mother Language Day, fostering a strong cultural connection even while away from home. BSO also creates a welcoming space for all CMU students—regardless of background—who are interested in exploring Bangladeshi culture through food, music, storytelling, and shared experiences. Members benefit from opportunities to grow as leaders by organizing events and taking part in community outreach. 				25 text alpha Kappa Delta Phi Sorority
			26 text Through a variety of philanthropic and social activities, alpha Kappa Delta Phi inspires its members to adopt important values such as leadership, empathy, and ambition. We always strive for excellence.
			27 text Since 2003, members have upheld these values through academic success, philanthropy, character development, and solid relationship-building skills. Our members are actively involved in many events throughout the year, allowing them to create lifelong bonds and consistently give back to the community.
			28 text We are the Carnegie Mellon University Pre-Associate Chapter of alpha Kappa Delta Phi Sorority, Inc., an international, Asian-interest (but not exclusive) organization. Since our charter in 2003, we’ve crossed over 200 sisters into our chapter (with one class per semester). Our sorority is committed to the five pillars of sisterhood, leadership, academic excellence, service, and Asian Awareness, and we strive to promote these values in everything that we do.

				38 text Kappa Phi Lambda Sorority
			39 text We, the sisters of the Kappa Phi Lambda Sorority, Incorporated, strive to strengthen sisterhood amongst women by providing service and promoting cultural diversity to our members and our community, thus securing the bond of kinship for posterity.
			40 text Kappa Phi Lambda Sorority is an Asian-interest sorority that was conceived through the notion of an organization that would provide a culturally sound and educationally inspiring grounding for Asian-American women. Although we are Asian-interest, we are not Asian-exclusive.
			41 text We are a cultural sorority with an emphasis on service and commitment to giving back to our members’ communities. As the Pi Chapter of Kappa Phi Lambda, we were rechartered on November 2018 on campus and achieved chapter status in January 2023.

				51 text Lambda Phi Epsilon Fraternity
			52 text Founded on March 24, 2002, the Carnegie Mellon chapter of Lambda Phi Epsilon was established by seventeen men committed to unifying and strengthening the Asian community at Carnegie Mellon University. What began as the Brotherhood of Asian-American Men (BAM) grew into a determined effort to bring ΛΦΕ to campus, culminating in their crossing into Eternal Brotherhood. As a social and service fraternity with Asian-American interests in mind, ΛΦΕ is grounded in the principles of wisdom, honor, and courage and is dedicated to fostering leadership, moral character, and lifelong bonds of brotherhood.
			53 text Since its founding, CMU ΛΦΕ has crossed over 140 brothers across multiple classes and continues to play an active role in cultural, service, and Greek life programming. With chapters nationwide, ΛΦΕ provides men of all ethnicities a space to unite around shared values and goals. Built on trust, sacrifice, and an enduring commitment to one another, the fraternity strives to perpetuate fellowship, respect, and Eternal Brotherhood for generations to come.

			18 container intro-text
				19 text Asian Christian Fellowship (ACF) is PCC’s college student ministry, and is made up of students from Pitt, CMU, and other schools in the Pittsburgh area. We are student-led under the supervision of Gordon Ott, an elder of PCC, and his wife Julie.
				20 text ACF is a cell-based ministry, where each cell group is single gendered and meets weekly to study the Bible, share, and encourage one another. Additionally, the whole fellowship meets each Friday night to worship, learn about and discuss the Bible, and to have fellowship. Most of our members also attend PCC on Sunday mornings, using a bus provided by the church.
				21 text Finally, outside of our core events, our members love to organize meals, meet-ups, jam sessions, and other fun events. We enjoy spending time together, whether to study, disciple, or to have fun, and pray that all we do would be to God’s glory.
				22 text Our hope is this website isn’t about how spiffy we are or how much we do, but rather how we are a body of believers who strive to be transformed from the inside out by the love of Jesus Christ.
				23 text We pray that college wouldn’t just be an educational and social time but also a time to grow closer to God, and we would love to get to know you and grow with you. Below are some ways you can get plugged in!

	27 heading Licensing Exams, Value: 1
		28 text Licensing Exams
	29 text In order to become an amateur radio operator in the United States, you must first pass one or more multiple-choice exams to obtain a license from the FCC. These exams cover basic theory of electronics and radio, as well as FCC rules, and are administered by groups of volunteer examiners around the country, including a group here at Carnegie Mellon. We offer exams for Technician, General, and Extra class licenses. You can take any or all of the exams for a single fee. Knowledge of Morse code is no longer required to obtain an amateur radio license in the U.S.

				158 container
					159 text Chhavi Yadav : Benchmarking Agent Susceptibility to Decomposition Attacks
					160 text Abstract
					161 text LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable and widely deployed, creating growing incentives for adversarial misuse in the real world. A key emerging threat is decomposition attacks, in which a harmful task is broken into simpler, benign subtasks that evade safety mechanisms when executed separately but cumulatively fulfill the malicious intent. Although recent benchmarks assess agent safety in multi-turn and multi-tool-use settings, they do not explicitly capture this form of decompositional misuse and may not represent realistic adversarial execution flows. To this end, we introduce DeCompBench, a benchmark designed specifically to evaluate agentic safety under decomposition attacks. DeCompBench is created with a decomposition-by-design principle using a graphical framework, and it enables harmful task decomposition into individually benign and executable subtasks with realistic workflows. Our experiments using a prompt-based LLM decomposer show that state-of-the-art agents exhibit high refusal rates on monolithic harmful tasks but significantly lower refusal rates on their decomposed variants, often inadvertently fulfilling the adversarial objectives. These findings underscore the need for safety evaluations against decomposition attacks and corresponding defenses. Our dataset is available at

Her work has been recognized with an NCWIT Collegiate Award (Finalist, 2025), an AAAI Doctoral Consortium Award (2025), a Rising Star in Data Science Award (2024), a Best Paper Award at the ICLR 2024 Privacy Workshop, and a Best Paper Honorable Mention at the NeurIPS 2019 ML4Health Workshop. 						28 text Director of Organizations
					29 text Welcome to the homepage of Carnegie Mellon University’s Director of Organizations. The Director of Organizations serves within the Student Government Executive Branch and is dedicated to supporting, and empowering student organizations across campus. In this role, the Director of Organizations oversees the new recognition process for student organizations seeking Student Government recognition, as well as the annual re-recognition process for 350+ recognized student organizations. The DoO also facilitates the bi-annual space allocation process, working to ensure equitable and effective access to campus space to student organizations.  Beyond these responsibilities, the Director of Organizations works closely with the Office of Student Involvement & Traditions to support the evolving needs of student organizations. Through collaboration, advocacy, and strategic planning, the DoO aims to strengthen the student organization ecosystem and foster a vibrant, inclusive, and engaged campus community. 						34 text The Center for Student Diversity & Inclusion
					35 text Inclusive Excellence has a singular place among the values of Carnegie Mellon University.
					36 text The Center for Student Diversity and Inclusion is a place for everyone. The Center actively cultivates a strong, diverse and inclusive community capable of living out our Carnegie Mellon values while advancing research, creativity and learning that changes the world. The Center offers programs and resources to enhance the student experience in dimensions such as access, personal development and success, campus climate and intergroup dialogue. We provide a centralized space for students looking to take a break between classes, hold meetings or study individually or with others.
